q: First time in Egypt. How much baksheesh do I give people like guards at the tombs or toilet attendants, and how hard should I haggle in Khan el-Khalili?
reference: Tipping (baksheesh) is expected almost everywhere in Egypt: small notes of roughly 5-20 EGP for toilet attendants, porters and guards who open a tomb or let you take a photo, and about 10% in restaurants even when a service charge is added. Keep a stack of small notes because change is often scarce. In Khan el-Khalili haggling is normal: counter well below the first price (often a third to a half of it), stay friendly, and be ready to walk away.

q: how do trains work in india for a tourist? how do i book, is sleeper class ok or should i get 3AC, and what is tatkal
reference: Book on the IRCTC website or app (foreigners can register with a foreign phone number and email) or at station counters; big stations have a foreign tourist quota office. Sleeper (SL) is cheap, non-air-conditioned open berths that get crowded; 3AC has air conditioning, bedding and fewer people and is the usual comfortable choice. Tatkal is a last-minute quota that opens the day before departure (10:00 for AC classes, 11:00 for non-AC) at a higher fare. Waitlisted (WL) tickets may never confirm, while RAC gets you on board with a shared berth.

q: Is Norway really that cashless? Going for 2 weeks incl. small towns up north, can I survive on just my Visa card?
reference: Yes. Norway is one of the most cashless countries: cards, especially contactless Visa and Mastercard, are accepted almost everywhere, including small shops, cafes, buses, ferries and even public toilets. Some places prefer not to handle cash at all. Make sure your card has a PIN, decline dynamic currency conversion and pay in NOK, and keep a little cash only as a backup.

q: Backpacking Uzbekistan in May. Do I have to register somewhere when I stay in a city, and are the fast trains between Tashkent, Samarkand and Bukhara worth it / how far ahead should I book?
reference: Foreigners must be registered for stays; hotels and licensed guesthouses do it automatically and give you a registration slip or online record, so keep these for your whole trip (gaps longer than a few days can mean fines). Many nationalities can enter visa-free for up to 30 days. The Afrosiyob high-speed trains are the best way between Tashkent, Samarkand (about 2 hours) and Bukhara (about 1.5 hours further) and are comfortable and cheap. They sell out, especially in spring, so book days or weeks ahead on the Uzbekistan Railways website or app.

q: first trip to china next month. will google maps and whatsapp work there, and can foreigners actually pay with alipay or wechat pay now?
reference: Google services (Maps, Gmail), WhatsApp, Instagram and many western sites are blocked on Chinese networks. A foreign SIM or eSIM on roaming usually bypasses the block because traffic goes through the home network; otherwise set up a VPN before you arrive. Use Amap (Gaode), Baidu Maps or Apple Maps for navigation. Alipay and WeChat Pay now accept foreign Visa and Mastercard cards after passport verification, with a small fee on larger payments; set them up before you go and still carry some cash as a backup.

q: renting a campervan in new zealand for 3 weeks. where are we allowed to freedom camp, and does it matter if the van has no toilet?
reference: Freedom camping is allowed only where councils or DOC permit it, and many towns ban it or restrict it to signed sites. Under the rules that took effect in 2023 (fully from 2024-25), a vehicle must be certified self-contained, with a fixed toilet, to freedom camp on council land; vans without a toilet must use campgrounds, holiday parks or DOC campsites. Fines are typically NZ$400 or more and rental companies pass them on. Apps like CamperMate show legal spots.

q: Going Athens to Santorini by ferry in late June. Where do they leave from, how long does it take, and do I need to book ahead or can I just turn up at the port?
reference: Most ferries to Santorini leave from Piraeus, with some from Rafina. High-speed boats take about 5 hours, conventional ferries 7-9 hours, usually stopping at other Cycladic islands. In late June it is wise to book a few days to weeks ahead, especially for fast boats, cabins or a car; deck tickets on big ferries rarely sell out completely. Buy on the operators' sites, an agent or a booking platform. Strong summer meltemi winds can delay or cancel smaller fast boats.

q: Heading to Ethiopia. Someone told me they tell time differently, like my bus 'at 12' is actually early morning?? how does that work
reference: Ethiopians traditionally count the 12 hours of the day from dawn (about 6 am) and the 12 hours of the night from dusk, so Ethiopian time runs six hours off the clock: 'one o'clock' is 7 am and 'twelve o'clock' in the morning is 6 am. A bus 'at 12' therefore usually means around 6 am. Always ask whether a time is in Ethiopian or 'ferenji' (foreign) time. Ethiopia also has its own calendar of 13 months, about 7-8 years behind the Gregorian one, with New Year on 11 September.

q: Cambodia: do I need US dollars or riel? should I bring cash from home and are the ATMs expensive
reference: Cambodia runs on both: prices in tourist areas, hotels and tours are mostly in US dollars, while riel is used for small change and cheap purchases, at about 4,000 riel to the dollar. Change under one dollar comes back in riel. Bring clean, untorn dollar notes since damaged ones are often refused. ATMs dispense dollars but usually add a fee of a few dollars per withdrawal, so take out larger amounts less often.

q: Weekend in Edinburgh. What should I see along the Royal Mile, and is the castle actually worth the ticket price?
reference: The Royal Mile runs from Edinburgh Castle down to the Palace of Holyroodhouse. Along it are St Giles' Cathedral, the Real Mary King's Close (underground streets), Camera Obscura and World of Illusions, Gladstone's Land, John Knox House and the Scottish Parliament at the bottom. The castle is worth it for most first visitors: the Honours of Scotland (crown jewels) and Stone of Destiny, St Margaret's Chapel, the views and the One O'Clock Gun; book online to save time. For free views, climb Arthur's Seat or Calton Hill.

q: where can i drink proper czech beer in prague without ending up in a tourist trap? looking for old-school pubs
reference: Classic pubs include U Zlatého tygra (an old regulars' pub in the Old Town), U Medvídků (historic brewery pub with its own beer), U Fleků (brewing since 1499, touristy but historic), Lokál (Pilsner Urquell from tanks with good Czech food) and U Hrocha in Malá Strana. Pivovarský dům is a good microbrewery. Prices drop and crowds thin quickly away from Old Town Square, and neighbourhoods like Vinohrady and Žižkov are full of local pubs.

q: Rainy day in Seoul. Which museums are worth it? We have the whole day
reference: The National Museum of Korea in Yongsan is huge, free and can fill most of a day, with the National Hangeul Museum next door. The War Memorial of Korea is close by and also free. Others: the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMCA Seoul, near Gyeongbokgung), the National Palace Museum and National Folk Museum inside the Gyeongbokgung area, and Leeum (Samsung's art museum) in Hannam-dong. COEX Mall with the Starfield Library is a good indoor fallback.

q: 3 days in Kraków. What should we see in the old town and Kazimierz, and is the Wieliczka salt mine worth half a day?
reference: In the Old Town: the Main Market Square with the Cloth Hall (Sukiennice) and St Mary's Basilica (Veit Stoss altarpiece, hourly trumpet call), then up to Wawel Castle and Cathedral. Kazimierz, the old Jewish quarter, has the Old Synagogue, the Remuh synagogue and cemetery, Plac Nowy with its zapiekanka stalls, and lively bars; across the river in Podgórze is Schindler's Factory museum. Wieliczka Salt Mine (UNESCO) is about 30 minutes away and is worth half a day for the carved chambers and the Chapel of St Kinga; tours are guided and take 2-3 hours.

q: staying in the old quarter in hanoi. where do i get the best pho and bun cha?
reference: For pho, well-known spots are Phở Gia Truyền (Phở Bát Đàn) on Bát Đàn street in the Old Quarter and Phở Thìn on Lò Đúc. For bún chả, Bún Chả Đắc Kim on Hàng Mành in the Old Quarter is a classic, and Bún Chả Hương Liên on Lê Văn Hưu is famous since Obama ate there. Most of these are cheap, busy at lunch, and close when they sell out.

q: Cape Town with our 6 and 9 year olds for a week. What are the best things to do with them?
reference: Good family picks: the Table Mountain Aerial Cableway (rotating car; check for wind closures), the penguin colony at Boulders Beach in Simon's Town, the Two Oceans Aquarium at the V&A Waterfront, Kirstenbosch Botanical Garden with its Tree Canopy Walkway, and Cape Point. Also the Iziko South African Museum and Planetarium, and a seal-spotting boat trip from Hout Bay. Muizenberg beach with its colourful huts has gentle surf for kids.

q: Which classic coffee houses in Vienna should I go to? Want the old-school experience, not a chain
reference: Famous traditional cafés include Café Central (grand vaulted hall in Palais Ferstel), Café Sacher (home of the Sachertorte), Café Landtmann by the Burgtheater, Café Hawelka (dark, bohemian), Café Sperl (old billiard tables), Demel (former court confectioner) and Café Prückel. Order a Melange or Einspänner; it comes with a glass of water, and you can linger for hours with newspapers.

q: I'm vegan and in Berlin for 4 days. Which vegan restaurants or cafes are worth going to?
reference: Berlin is one of the most vegan-friendly cities in the world, and Friedrichshain, Kreuzberg, Neukölln and Prenzlauer Berg have the densest choice. Long-standing names include Kopps (vegan restaurant in Mitte), Brammibal's Donuts, and vegan döner shops such as Vöner. Many ordinary cafés and döner stands also have clearly marked vegan options. Opening days and times change, so check a listing before going.

q: who was Ada Lovelace?
reference: Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) was an English mathematician, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron. She worked with Charles Babbage on his planned Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer. Her 1843 notes on a translated article about the engine include a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, often called the first computer program. She also foresaw that such machines could handle symbols such as music, not just numbers.

q: How deep is Lake Baikal and how old is it?
reference: Lake Baikal in southern Siberia, Russia, is the deepest lake in the world at about 1,640 m (1,642 m at its deepest point). It is also the oldest, at about 25-30 million years. It holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water, more than all the North American Great Lakes together, and has many endemic species such as the Baikal seal.

q: tell me about namibia
reference: Namibia is a country in south-western Africa on the Atlantic coast, with Windhoek as its capital and about 3 million people, making it one of the least densely populated countries. It was a German colony (German South West Africa), then run by South Africa, and became independent in 1990. Its landscapes include the Namib Desert with the Sossusvlei dunes, the Skeleton Coast and Etosha National Park. The economy relies heavily on mining (diamonds, uranium) and tourism; English is the official language.

q: When was the Great Wall of China built? Was it all built at once?
reference: No. Walls were built by different Chinese states from around the 7th century BC; after unifying China in 221 BC, Qin Shi Huang linked and extended several of them. Later dynasties built and rebuilt walls, and most of the brick-and-stone sections tourists visit today (such as Badaling and Mutianyu) are from the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). Counting all branches and periods, the walls total about 21,000 km.

q: highest mountain in africa? how tall and where
reference: Mount Kilimanjaro, in north-eastern Tanzania near the border with Kenya, is Africa's highest mountain at about 5,895 m (19,341 ft). Its summit is Uhuru Peak on the Kibo cone. It is a dormant volcano with three cones (Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira) and the highest free-standing mountain in the world.

q: Tell me about Madagascar
reference: Madagascar is the fourth-largest island in the world, in the Indian Ocean off south-east Africa, with Antananarivo as its capital and around 30 million people. It split from the Indian subcontinent around 88 million years ago, so most of its wildlife is found nowhere else, including lemurs, many chameleons and baobab species. It was a French colony until independence in 1960; Malagasy and French are official languages. It is one of the world's poorest countries and a leading producer of vanilla.

q: who was Mansa Musa and was he really the richest man ever?
reference: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali Empire in West Africa in the early 14th century (roughly 1312-1337). He is famous for his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca with a huge caravan carrying so much gold that his spending in Cairo depressed the value of gold there for years. He expanded the empire, including Timbuktu and Gao, and built mosques such as Djinguereber, making Timbuktu a centre of Islamic learning. He is often called the richest person in history, but his wealth cannot be measured meaningfully against modern fortunes.

q: When did the Chernobyl disaster happen and what actually caused the explosion?
reference: It happened on 26 April 1986 at reactor No. 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant near Pripyat in Soviet Ukraine. During a poorly run safety test at low power, operators broke safety rules, and flaws in the RBMK reactor design (a positive void coefficient and control rods whose graphite tips briefly increased reactivity) caused a power surge. This led to a steam explosion and a graphite fire that spread radioactive material over much of Europe. Two workers died in the explosion and 28 more from acute radiation sickness within months; a 30 km exclusion zone remains.

q: my friend just got bitten on the ankle by a snake on a trail in costa rica. it's swelling fast. what do we do? should we use a tourniquet or suck the venom out?
reference: No tourniquet, no cutting, no sucking, no ice. Keep him calm and as still as possible, remove rings, boots or tight items before the swelling grows, splint the leg and keep it at roughly heart level, and get him to a hospital with antivenom as fast as possible, carrying him if you can. Note the time of the bite and, if seen safely, what the snake looked like, but do not try to catch it. Most dangerous Costa Rican snakes are vipers (like the fer-de-lance), so watch for spreading swelling, bleeding and shock on the way.

q: hiking in 38 degrees and my friend has stopped sweating, he's hot, confused and slurring. what do i do right now
reference: Hot skin, no sweating and confusion means heatstroke, which is life-threatening. Get him into shade at once, remove extra clothing and cool him as fast as possible: immerse him in cool water if there is any, otherwise soak him with water and fan him, and put cold packs or wet cloths on the neck, armpits and groin. Only give sips of water if he is fully awake and can swallow; never force fluids if he is confused or vomiting. Keep cooling while you get help and evacuate him, and watch for seizures or collapse.

q: we're at 4,200 m in the himalaya. my partner has a splitting headache, keeps vomiting and is stumbling when she walks. can we wait until morning?
reference: No. Severe headache with vomiting and loss of coordination at altitude points to high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE), which can kill within hours. Descend immediately, at least 300-1,000 m, even at night if it can be done safely, and never let her go up or stay alone. If available, give dexamethasone and oxygen or use a portable hyperbaric bag, but these only buy time for the descent. Acetazolamide helps milder altitude sickness but is not enough here.

q: got bitten by a stray dog in rural india. it broke the skin a bit. do i really need rabies shots and how fast?
reference: Yes. Wash the wound straight away with soap and running water for about 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic such as iodine or alcohol. Any bite or scratch that breaks the skin from a stray in a rabies country needs post-exposure treatment as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours: a course of rabies vaccine (several doses over 2-4 weeks) and, if you were not vaccinated before, rabies immunoglobulin injected around the wound. Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so do not wait. Also check your tetanus status.

q: My friend ate something with peanuts, her lips are swelling and she's wheezing. She has an EpiPen. What do I do?
reference: Treat this as anaphylaxis and use the EpiPen now: inject into the outer thigh (through clothing is fine) and hold it in place for a few seconds, then call emergency help. Lay her flat with legs raised, or let her sit up if breathing is easier that way, and do not make her stand or walk. If there is no improvement after 5-15 minutes and a second injector is available, give it. She must go to hospital even if she gets better, because symptoms can return hours later; antihistamines do not replace adrenaline.

q: cut my hand really deep on broken glass and it won't stop bleeding. how do i stop it and do i need stitches?
reference: Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing and keep pressing without lifting for at least 10 minutes; if blood soaks through, add more layers on top rather than removing the first. Raise the hand above heart level. If bleeding is spurting or won't stop with firm pressure, keep pressing and get urgent help; a tourniquet on the upper arm is a last resort for life-threatening bleeding. A deep or gaping cut, glass possibly still in the wound, or numbness or trouble moving fingers needs a doctor for stitches and to check tendons and nerves, ideally within hours; also check your tetanus status.

q: How do vaccines actually train your immune system? And how is an mRNA vaccine different, does it change your DNA?
reference: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form or piece of a pathogen (an antigen), so it produces antibodies and memory B and T cells without you getting sick; on real exposure the response is much faster and stronger. Traditional vaccines use killed or weakened germs or purified proteins. An mRNA vaccine delivers instructions, wrapped in lipid nanoparticles, that let your cells briefly make one viral protein (for example the coronavirus spike); the mRNA breaks down within days. It never enters the cell nucleus and cannot change your DNA.

q: why is the sky blue but sunsets are orange and red?
reference: Sunlight is scattered by air molecules (Rayleigh scattering), and short blue wavelengths scatter much more than long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from all over the sky. It doesn't look violet because sunlight contains less violet, some is absorbed high up, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. At sunset sunlight passes through far more atmosphere, so most of the blue is scattered away before it reaches you, leaving orange and red.

q: How does my phone's GPS know where I am when I have no signal or internet at all?
reference: GPS doesn't use the phone network. Satellites constantly broadcast their precise time and orbit position; your phone's GPS receiver measures how long the signals from at least four satellites took to arrive and works out its position (and corrects its own clock) by trilateration. Internet only helps through assisted GPS, which downloads satellite data to get a fix faster. Without internet the first fix can take longer, and you need offline maps to see where you are on a map.

q: Why is jet lag worse flying east than west, and does melatonin actually help?
reference: Your body clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain) is reset mainly by light and only shifts about an hour a day, so after crossing time zones it stays out of step with local time, causing poor sleep, daytime tiredness and stomach upsets. Flying east is harder because you have to advance the clock (sleep earlier), while the natural body clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours and adapts more easily to later times. Melatonin taken near local bedtime at the destination reduces jet lag for many people, especially after eastward flights over several time zones; timing daylight exposure also helps.

q: How do tides work? why are there two high tides a day and not one
reference: Tides come mainly from the Moon's gravity pulling unevenly across the Earth: the side facing the Moon is pulled more than Earth's centre and the far side less, so the oceans form two bulges, one facing the Moon and one opposite. As the Earth rotates through both bulges, most coasts get two high and two low tides roughly every 24 hours and 50 minutes, because the Moon moves along its orbit meanwhile. The Sun adds a smaller effect: when Sun and Moon line up (new and full moon) you get bigger spring tides, and at quarter moons smaller neap tides.

q: how does a microwave oven heat food? and why is it hot on the edges and still frozen in the middle sometimes
reference: A magnetron produces microwaves (around 2.45 GHz) that bounce around inside the metal box. Their rapidly alternating electric field makes polar molecules, mainly water, keep turning to line up with it, and this motion becomes heat (dielectric heating). Microwaves only penetrate a few centimetres, so the centre heats by conduction from the outside, and standing waves create hot and cold spots, which is why there's a turntable. Ice absorbs microwaves poorly compared with liquid water, so thawed edges heat up fast while frozen parts stay frozen.

q: alligator vs crocodile, how do you tell them apart?
reference: Alligators have a broad, rounded U-shaped snout, while crocodiles have a narrower, pointed V-shaped one. With the mouth closed, a crocodile's teeth on both jaws show, including a big fourth tooth on the lower jaw, whereas an alligator's upper jaw hides most of the lower teeth. Alligators live mainly in fresh water in the south-eastern US and China, while crocodiles are spread through the tropics and tolerate salt water thanks to salt glands. Alligators are usually darker, and some crocodiles (saltwater, Nile) are more aggressive.

q: Got a fever in Southeast Asia and it might be dengue. Should I take ibuprofen or paracetamol? Whats the difference
reference: Take paracetamol (acetaminophen). Both lower fever and ease pain, but ibuprofen, aspirin and other NSAIDs also reduce platelet function and can irritate the stomach, which raises the risk of bleeding in dengue, so they should be avoided until dengue is ruled out. Ibuprofen also reduces inflammation, so it is often better for sprains or dental pain when dengue isn't a concern. Paracetamol is gentle on the stomach but has no anti-inflammatory effect and damages the liver in overdose, so stick to the label limit (usually 4 g a day for adults). See a doctor if fever lasts or warning signs like bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting appear.

q: what's the actual difference between a lager and an ale?
reference: The difference is the yeast and how it ferments. Ales use top-fermenting yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) at warmer temperatures, around 15-24 °C, which ferments quickly and gives fruity, complex flavours. Lagers use bottom-fermenting yeast (Saccharomyces pastorianus) at cooler temperatures, around 7-13 °C, followed by weeks of cold storage (lagering), which gives a cleaner, crisper taste. Colour and strength don't decide it: stouts are ales, and bocks and dark lagers are lagers.

q: First safari, going in August. Masai Mara in Kenya or the Serengeti in Tanzania? We really want to see the migration river crossings
reference: They are one ecosystem split by the border, and in August the wildebeest migration is usually in the northern Serengeti and the Masai Mara, with Mara River crossings from about July to October. The Masai Mara is smaller, easy to reach from Nairobi, often cheaper per day and very good for dense game viewing, but it can get crowded with vehicles at crossings. The Serengeti is much bigger and wilder; the northern part (around Kogatende) has crossings with fewer vehicles but costs more and is more remote. Crossings are never guaranteed, so allow several days either way.

q: hurricane vs typhoon vs cyclone, is there any difference or is it the same thing?
reference: They are the same weather phenomenon, a strong tropical cyclone, with different names by region. In the North Atlantic and the north-eastern Pacific it is a hurricane, in the north-western Pacific a typhoon, and in the South Pacific and Indian Ocean a (tropical) cyclone. The hurricane threshold is sustained winds of about 119 km/h (74 mph). Storms spin counter-clockwise in the northern hemisphere and clockwise in the southern.

q: baking soda vs baking powder? can I swap one for the other in a cake recipe
reference: Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate; it needs an acid in the recipe (buttermilk, yogurt, lemon juice, brown sugar) to release carbon dioxide, and it is about three to four times stronger. Baking powder is baking soda already mixed with a dry acid (such as cream of tartar) and starch, so it only needs moisture, and double-acting powder releases more gas when heated. You can replace 1 teaspoon of baking powder with about 1/4 teaspoon of baking soda plus 1/2 teaspoon of cream of tartar. Swapping soda for powder needs about three times as much powder and can affect taste.

q: Road trip of 640 km. The car uses 6.8 litres per 100 km and fuel costs 1.85 euros a litre. If 4 of us split the fuel, how much does each person pay?
reference: Fuel needed: 640 × 6.8 / 100 = 43.52 litres. Cost: 43.52 × 1.85 = 80.51 euros. Split four ways that is about 20.13 euros each.

q: my flight leaves Dubai (UTC+4) at 02:15 on Tuesday and takes 14 h 30 min to Los Angeles (UTC-7). what day and local time do I land?
reference: Departure is Monday 22:15 UTC. Adding 14 h 30 min gives Tuesday 12:45 UTC. Los Angeles is UTC-7, so you land at 05:45 on Tuesday, local time.

q: I need 300 euros. The exchange booth gives 1.12 euros per pound with no fee. The ATM gives 1.16 euros per pound but my bank charges a flat 4 pound fee. Which is cheaper and by how much?
reference: Booth: 300 / 1.12 = £267.86. ATM: 300 / 1.16 = £258.62, plus the £4 fee = £262.62. The ATM is cheaper by about £5.24.

q: Desert hike of 18 km at about 3.6 km/h. I want 0.5 litres of water per hour of walking plus a 1 litre reserve. How many 1.5 litre bottles should I carry?
reference: The hike takes 18 / 3.6 = 5 hours, so you drink 5 × 0.5 = 2.5 litres; with the 1 litre reserve that is 3.5 litres. 3.5 / 1.5 = 2.33, so carry 3 bottles (4.5 litres).

q: Want to run a half marathon (21.1 km) in 1 hour 55 minutes. What pace per km is that? And what would my finish time be at 5:15 per km?
reference: 1 h 55 min is 115 minutes; 115 / 21.1 = 5.45 minutes per km, which is about 5:27 per km. At 5:15 per km (5.25 minutes), 21.1 × 5.25 = 110.8 minutes, a finish time of about 1:50:47.

q: 3 of us share a flat that costs 2,100 a month. The bedrooms are 18, 12 and 10 square metres. If we split the rent by room size, how much does each person pay?
reference: Total bedroom area is 18 + 12 + 10 = 40 m², so the rent is 2,100 / 40 = 52.50 per m². The 18 m² room pays 945, the 12 m² room 630 and the 10 m² room 525, which adds up to 2,100.

q: How did the Black Death change Europe afterwards? Like the economy, wages, serfdom, the church
reference: The plague of 1347-1351 killed roughly a third to a half of Europe's population. The labour shortage raised wages and gave peasants bargaining power; despite laws trying to freeze wages (such as England's Statute of Labourers, 1351) and revolts like the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381, serfdom declined in western Europe while land became cheaper and living standards of survivors improved. The Church's authority suffered because it could not explain or stop the plague and lost many clergy, and there were violent persecutions of Jews and movements like the flagellants. Some historians link these shifts to later labour-saving innovation and social change.

q: what happened to the aral sea? why did it shrink so much and what did that do to the people living around it
reference: The Aral Sea, once one of the four largest lakes in the world, began shrinking in the 1960s when Soviet planners diverted its two feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton and other crops in Central Asia. By the 2010s it had lost about 90% of its volume and split into separate lakes. The fishing industry collapsed, leaving ports like Moynaq and Aralsk far from water, and winds blow salt and pesticide-laden dust from the dry seabed, linked to respiratory illness and other health problems, while the local climate became more extreme. In Kazakhstan the Kok-Aral dam (2005) has partly restored the small North Aral Sea and its fishery.

q: Is intermittent fasting actually better for losing weight than just eating less every day? what have the trials found
reference: Randomised trials comparing intermittent fasting (alternate-day fasting, 5:2, or time-restricted eating) with ordinary daily calorie restriction mostly find similar weight loss when total calories are similar, with no clear extra metabolic benefit. Examples include a year-long alternate-day fasting trial (2017) and a 2022 NEJM trial of time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction. Its main advantage is that some people find it easier to stick to, while others drop out more. Animal studies show larger benefits than human trials have confirmed.

q: How did Gutenberg's printing press change Europe? Was it really behind the Reformation?
reference: Gutenberg's movable-type press (Mainz, around 1450) cut the cost of books dramatically, and by 1500 millions of copies had been printed across hundreds of European towns. Printing let Martin Luther's writings from 1517 onward spread rapidly and cheaply, especially in German, so it was a key enabler of the Reformation, though not its only cause. It also standardised texts and spellings, helped scientific results spread and be checked, boosted literacy and vernacular languages, and carried Renaissance humanism across Europe.

q: Does rapamycin really extend lifespan? what's the evidence in animals vs in humans
reference: Rapamycin inhibits mTOR, a nutrient-sensing pathway, and extends lifespan in yeast, worms and flies. In mice the NIA Interventions Testing Program showed (Harrison et al., 2009) that it extends lifespan even when started late in life, with larger effects in females, a result repeated in several studies. In humans there is no lifespan evidence: small trials show that low-dose rapamycin analogues improved vaccine responses in older adults, but long-term benefit is unproven. Side effects at higher doses include immune suppression, mouth ulcers and raised blood sugar and lipids.

q: how do 12 seed words turn into all my wallet addresses? like what is BIP39 and how does the wallet get keys from it
reference: BIP39 encodes random entropy (128 bits for 12 words) plus a short checksum as words from a fixed list of 2048 words. The words and an optional passphrase are run through PBKDF2 (2048 rounds of HMAC-SHA512) to make a 512-bit seed. BIP32 turns that seed into a master key and a tree of child keys that can be derived deterministically, and BIP44 paths such as m/44'/60'/0'/0/0 pick each account and address. Because every key can be regenerated from the words, anyone who has them controls all the funds.

q: What makes SHA-256 a one-way function? Why can't someone just reverse the hash to get the input?
reference: SHA-256 pads the input and processes it in 512-bit blocks through 64 rounds of bitwise operations, rotations and modular additions, producing a 256-bit output. Information is mixed so thoroughly and so much is discarded (infinitely many inputs map to each output) that there is no known way to work backwards; the only approach is guessing inputs, which for a random input means about 2^256 tries. A tiny change in the input changes about half the output bits (avalanche effect). That is why it is used for Bitcoin mining, transaction IDs and addresses.

q: What are gas fees on Ethereum, and what changed with EIP-1559? Why does some ETH get burned?
reference: Gas measures the computation and storage a transaction uses, and the fee is the gas used times the price per unit of gas. EIP-1559 (London upgrade, August 2021) added a protocol-set base fee per block that rises or falls by up to 12.5% depending on whether the previous block was above or below the gas target, plus an optional priority fee (tip) for the block producer. The base fee is burned rather than paid to miners or validators, so they can't profit from manipulating it, and burning reduces ETH supply. Blocks can also temporarily stretch to twice the target size, making fees more predictable.

q: What is a Merkle tree and why do blockchains use them?
reference: A Merkle tree hashes data items (for example transactions) in pairs, then hashes those hashes in pairs, up to a single root hash. A block header stores only the Merkle root, so changing any transaction changes the root and is detected. A light client can check that a transaction is in a block with a short Merkle proof of about log2(n) hashes instead of downloading the whole block (Bitcoin's simplified payment verification). Ethereum uses Merkle Patricia tries for its state, transactions and receipts.

q: What did Vitalik mean by a 'rollup-centric' roadmap for Ethereum? Why focus on rollups instead of sharding everything?
reference: In his October 2020 post 'A rollup-centric Ethereum roadmap', Vitalik Buterin argued that Ethereum should scale mainly through layer-2 rollups (optimistic and ZK), which execute transactions off-chain and post compressed data and proofs to layer 1. Layer 1 then focuses on security and on providing cheap data space for rollups, so sharding shifts from execution shards to data sharding (later proto-danksharding with EIP-4844 blobs in 2024 and full danksharding). The reasons were that rollups already worked and could scale sooner, inherit Ethereum's security, and keep L1 simpler.

q: whats the blockchain scalability trilemma vitalik talks about, and how is sharding supposed to get around it?
reference: The trilemma says a simple blockchain can only get two of three properties: decentralisation (nodes run on ordinary hardware), scalability (processing more than one ordinary node could), and security (resisting attackers controlling a large share of resources). Traditional chains like Bitcoin and early Ethereum pick decentralisation and security, high-throughput chains give up decentralisation, and multi-chain setups weaken security. Sharding tries to get all three by splitting the work among randomly chosen committees of validators, using data availability sampling and fraud or validity proofs so each node checks only a small part while the whole chain stays secure.
